newsitem.title: USA: Republicans call on Clinton to take lead on CPI.
newsitem.headline: Republicans call on Clinton to take lead on CPI.

text.p: Two top Republicans Sunday called for President Clinton to take the lead in making changes to the consumer price index (CPI), a politically sensitive move because it would cut some popular government benefits.

The remarks by House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich and his Senate counterpart, Pete Domenici, were another piece of evidence the Republicans are not willing to take the blame for cutting such benefits without Clinton sharing the criticism.
"The ball's in the President's hands. If he wants to make the CPI more accurate, Republicans will be there to support him," Kasich told NBC television's "Meet the Press" program.

"I believe it is impossible to objectively analyze and change ... the CPI, if that is necessary, without the leadership of the president," New Mexico Republican Domenici told CNN's "Late Edition" program.

The seemingly arcane question of changing the CPI, the nation's key measure of inflation, has become a major issue in Washington because of a recent report that suggested that the index overstates inflation by 1.1 percentage points.

The report, prepared by a commission chaired by Stanford economist Michael Boskin, last week recommended a number of steps that would reduce the CPI and in turn cut payments in those government programs that are linked to the index.
Among these is the Social Security retirement program for the elderly as well as various veterans' benefit programs.
The issue has become a part of the debate in Washington over how to balance the federal budget because of the huge weight such programs have in the budegt.

Republicans, having taken a beating from Clinton during the U.S. election campaign over their plans to reform the popular Medicare health care program for the elderly, are wary of being tarred on any other reform efforts.

Domenici and Kasich said the question of changing the CPI should be left to experts, arguing that what was important was to have an accurate index. "This is not a political decision. This is about getting the numbers right," Kasich said.
But, in a tacit admission of how politically ticklish the issue is, Kasich said the Republican-controlled Congress was not prepared to try to make the changes alone.

"If (Clinton) doesn't want to do it, we're probably going to be out there criticizing him for not wanting to get this right," added Kasich, an Ohio Republican. "But we're just not going to walk out there by ourselves."

The Clinton administration has said it would study the Boskin report, along with the views of other experts and the Labor Deparement's Bureau of Labor Statistics, which compiles the index, before deciding what to do.
